summary:
Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer is an interactive educational game designed to introduce children aged 7–12 to space exploration and the challenges of managing lunar and Martian outposts.
Our goal is to make learning about space both realistic and fun. Through a cozy, interactive environment, children can explore, experiment, and discover without feeling overwhelmed by complex scientific concepts.
Players can customize their experience with cosmetic items, tackle STEM-focused minigames, and collaborate with friends in Co-op Mode. Our 3D Story Mode offers a world to freely explore, encouraging curiosity and learning at each player's own pace.
From driving rovers and repairing communication systems to completing missions and managing outpost resources, players experience different aspects of space exploration through hands-on activities and meaningful decisions.
Ultimately, we want children to see science and engineering not simply as subjects to study, but as exciting challenges to experience. Our mission is to inspire the next generation of explorers through play, discovery, and experimentation.
details:
Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer

Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer is a browser-based educational game designed to introduce children aged 7–12 to space exploration and the engineering challenges of establishing and maintaining lunar and Martian outposts.

Our central idea is simple: instead of just teaching children about the systems that keep astronauts alive, let them experience the decisions involved in operating those systems themselves.

How It Works

Players can embark on a 14-Sol expedition to either Mars or the Moon, where they must manage an outpost and balance essential resources, including oxygen, water, food, battery capacity and radiation exposure.

Before beginning an expedition, players must make engineering decisions within an 80 kg launch-payload restriction. They can select from five physical infrastructure upgrades: regolith radiation shielding, additional solar arrays, an upgraded water recycler, battery storage and greenhouse grow lights. Each has a different mass and benefit, forcing players to prioritize what their mission needs most.

Throughout the expedition, environmental conditions and unexpected events influence resource production and consumption. Solar power can be reduced by dust and poor illumination, radiation events can threaten the crew, and insufficient power can affect life-support and food-production systems. Players must anticipate problems, manage reserves and adapt their strategies to keep their outpost functioning.

The experience extends beyond resource management through nine solo mission types, two cooperative challenges, and a separate 3D Story Mode. Players can perform precision landings, drive rovers, repair base systems, explore caves, restore communications, rescue astronauts, mine asteroids, survive meteor showers and complete a final evacuation. Co-op activities encourage teamwork, while Story Mode gives players a separate Martian environment to explore and discover.

Players can also unlock equipment through successful missions, earn Tech Points for cosmetic customization, personalize their astronauts and maintain mission records. This separates gameplay progression from cosmetic rewards: engineering advantages are earned through accomplishments rather than purchased with currency.

Scientific Foundation and Accuracy

Scientific grounding was one of our most important design considerations. We incorporated representative figures and concepts from several NASA sources:

  • NASA BVAD and ISS Environmental Control and Life Support Systems (ECLSS) references inform oxygen, water, food and recycling mechanics.
  • Curiosity's REMS instrument informs Martian temperature conditions and dust-related reductions in solar power.
  • Curiosity's RAD instrument informs radiation exposure.
  • LRO Diviner and CRaTER data inform lunar illumination and radiation considerations.
  • NASA's DONKI Solar Energetic Particle API can provide space-weather information, with an archived-event fallback when live data is unavailable.

We also included an in-game scientific traceability section explaining the references and the simplified equations behind the simulation. Numerical values are curated, representative figures within published ranges, rather than direct real-time measurements for every simulated day. This allows us to maintain scientific relevance while making the simulation understandable and enjoyable for our target audience.

Educational Benefits and Intended Impact

We want children to develop an intuitive understanding of how interconnected space-mission systems are. A decision that improves food production might increase water and electricity demand. Additional radiation protection might compete with other hardware within the launch-mass limit. These relationships encourage systems thinking, resource management, problem-solving and engineering prioritization.

Beyond the simulation, cooperative missions encourage communication and teamwork, while exploration and minigames make scientific concepts approachable through experimentation and play.

Our intended impact is to make STEM education more engaging and inspire children to become curious about engineering, astronomy and future space exploration. We believe children learn particularly well when they are given the opportunity to experiment, make decisions and observe consequences rather than simply memorize information.

Technology and Development

The project was developed as a self-contained browser-based application using HTML, CSS and JavaScript.

Its implementation includes:

  • Canvas-based interactive minigames.
  • Bundled Three.js and WebGL for the 3D Story Mode.
  • Browser local storage for settings, progression, records and saved story progress.
  • Web Audio API for synthesized sound effects and an original soundtrack.
  • NASA DONKI API integration for optional live space-weather information.

The game does not require specialized hardware or additional peripherals. It runs in a modern browser, with WebGL required for the 3D experience.

Creativity and Design Considerations

Our biggest challenge was finding the balance between scientific realism and accessibility for children aged 7–12. We wanted to avoid both oversimplifying space exploration into meaningless activities and overwhelming young players with complicated engineering calculations.

We approached this by combining a resource-management simulation with interactive missions, cooperative gameplay, exploration, customization and a welcoming atmosphere. We also considered accessibility through adjustable controls, text sizing, contrast, color palettes, performance settings and audio preferences.

Another important design decision was keeping engineering decisions meaningful. Physical infrastructure is constrained by launch mass, mission equipment is earned through successful operations, and Tech Points are reserved for cosmetics. This encourages players to understand the consequences of engineering choices rather than treating every upgrade as an ordinary shop purchase.

Ultimately, Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer is our attempt to turn the challenges of sustaining an extraterrestrial outpost into an interactive learning experience. We want children to see space exploration not merely as something fascinating to watch, but as something they can actively understand, experiment with and imagine themselves participating in.
